label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
problem_in_my_words: The author could not show an idea that is a movement on a still slide, so he had to narrate every arrow himself; a team of agents let him press play and keep changing the result until the last hour.
why: The factory pitch is clear and the empty chair for security teases, but I was pulled in by the loop, not the roster; a list of role names (deck, motion, studio) tells me nothing about what each would do for my small publication, and the chapter never says who the nine are to me.
my_sentence: I want my reader to understand [one idea], and after reading I want them to be able to [one action].

by_section.why: The voice note is vivid and human, and the still-versus-movement problem is stated plainly. It is a presenter's problem, though, so I had to translate it to my own: a story whose point is a process.
by_section.quote: The idea was a movement. The slide was a still. I was the bit in between.

by_section.why: The long quoted passage about users and agents finding gold assumes I know what the building animation is and what the gold is. I do not, and I have never run an agent. The 18:26 detail is good but 'the thing that made it was still running, and still listening' is vague about what that thing is.
by_section.quote: Normal users come in and do things: they go where they're supposed to go.

by_section.why: This is the section that maps onto my newsroom: see it, ask again, see it again, with the editor looking. Times are specific and credible. 'The player' appears before it is defined, a small snag.
by_section.quote: See it, ask for it differently, see it again.

by_section.why: A detour to a named talk and an honest caveat that the day did not fully live up to it. It slows the momentum and does not raise the stakes for a reader who does not know the reference.
by_section.quote: Creators need an immediate connection to what they create.

by_section.why: The definition is modest and concrete: one objective, nine agents, one job and one page of rules each, taken apart after. The 'Words on this page' gloss helps. I wanted one line on why a team beats one agent. The empty chair is an effective hook.
by_section.quote: Nine of them, each with one job and one page of rules.

by_section.why: Short, doable, asks for one sentence with an audience and an outcome. 'That sentence is your first brief' is the right promise. I could write it in under a minute.
by_section.quote: Write down the one idea you want somebody to understand, and what they should be able to do after.

cut: Consider trimming the Bret Victor section to two lines, or moving it to the chapter's end notes. Cut or paraphrase the gold-finding quote to one sentence for a reader who has not seen the talk.
best_line: I talked over my own pictures.
worst_moment: Pressing play: the quoted animation passage about normal users and agents finding gold. It presumes context the reader does not have, and for a non-expert it is the point where the chapter sounds like a security talk rather than my problem.
notes: My question is whether a team could run my newsroom with me as the signing editor. The chapter hints at it (the editor asks, the team changes things) but never says that the human decides, so I am not yet sure the answer is yes. One sentence in the factory section naming the editor's role would help. The word 'brief' is used without being explained until later.
